results.result: Regenerative potential in H. diminuta is regionally limited to the neck, which is both necessary and sufficient for proglottid regeneration. Anterior fragments containing the neck (with or without the head) regenerate proglottids, while body-only fragments fail to regenerate despite being able to grow in length.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C46-C48, C52, C54, C58-C59 collectively demonstrate through amputation experiments (Figure 1) that only neck-containing fragments regenerate proglottids. The data show quantitative regeneration (383 proglottids from 2mm neck fragments) and clear negative results for body-only and head-only fragments, with appropriate controls and replication.

results.result: The head is required to maintain the neck and enable persistent regeneration. While decapitated fragments can regenerate proglottids after the first amputation, re-amputation abrogates regeneration as the neck cannot be maintained without the head.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by serial amputation experiments (Figure 1f-g, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) showing that fragments with heads can regenerate through at least four rounds of amputation, while decapitated fragments lose regenerative capacity after the first round. The observation that the neck eventually becomes entirely proglottidized without the head provides mechanistic insight.

results.result: Regeneration potential is asymmetric across the neck anterior-posterior axis with a strong anterior bias, as most-anterior neck fragments regenerate more proglottids than middle or posterior neck fragments.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by quantitative data from subdivided neck experiments (Figure 1h-i) showing differential regenerative capacity along the A-P axis. The statistical analysis and replication appear adequate, though the mechanism underlying this gradient is not yet elucidated.

results.result: Cycling somatic cells are distributed throughout the entire tapeworm body, including in regeneration-incompetent regions, with no evidence that stem cells are restricted to the regeneration-competent neck.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C74, C76, C8 are supported by F-ara-EdU labeling and FISH for mcm2/h2b (Figure 2a-b) showing cycling cells throughout the body including head, neck, and posterior proglottids. This distribution is inconsistent with a model where regenerative capacity is determined solely by stem cell localization.

results.result: Exposure to 200 Gy x-irradiation depletes cycling cells by 91±6%, abrogates growth and regeneration, and is lethal to H. diminuta. RNA-seq identified 683 irradiation-sensitive transcripts that were validated by WISH.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by quantitative cycling cell counts (Figure 2c-d), phenotypic analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and transcriptomic data with validation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). The approach is sound for identifying cycling cell markers, though irradiation may have secondary effects beyond stem cell depletion as acknowledged in C139.

results.result: Among 194 irradiation-sensitive transcripts with clear WISH patterns, 63% were expressed in the neck parenchyma in various patterns, with 13% showing patterns similar to cycling cell markers h2b and mcm2. All neck parenchyma transcripts were also found throughout the worm body.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C89 are supported by systematic WISH screening (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1) with clear categorization of expression patterns. The finding that all neck parenchyma transcripts are also expressed posteriorly (C88) is critical for the conclusion that stem cells are not restricted to the neck.

results.result: Double FISH experiments revealed transcriptional heterogeneity within the cycling cell compartment, with some transcripts co-expressed in all cycling cells, others in subsets of cycling cells, and some in both cycling and non-cycling cells, suggesting lineage-committed progenitors.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C94 are supported by dFISH data (Figure 3d, Figure 3—figure supplement 3) showing diverse co-expression patterns. The proposal that genes like HDt_10981 and ppt1 represent lineage-committed progenitors (C93) is reasonable speculation based on the data, though functional validation would strengthen this interpretation.

results.result: RNAi knockdown of cycling cell genes h2b, zmym3, and pogzl resulted in diminished growth and regeneration, severely reduced proliferative cells, and fewer mcm2+ cells, demonstrating these genes are necessary for cycling cell maintenance and/or function.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C100 are supported by RNAi experiments with multiple readouts: growth measurements (Figure 4b-c), F-ara-EdU incorporation (Figure 4d-e), and mcm2 WISH (Figure 4f). Knockdown was confirmed by qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This represents the first functional validation of stem cell genes in H. diminuta.

results.result: Cycling cell transcripts zmym3 and pogzl are expressed throughout the entire tapeworm body by WISH and FISH, including in posterior gonadal tissues and somatic parenchymal cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by WISH/FISH data (Figure 4g, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b-c, Figure 4—figure supplement 2) showing expression from anterior to posterior. This distribution further argues against a neck-specific stem cell population explaining regenerative capacity.

results.result: RNA-seq of neck A-P axis identified 461 anterior-enriched and 241 anterior-depleted transcripts, but 88% of anterior-enriched transcripts were not irradiation-sensitive, suggesting A-P polarized signals arise predominantly in non-cycling compartments. Analysis failed to reveal an anteriorly biased stem cell subpopulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C112 are supported by RNA-seq data (Supplementary file 1d), WISH validation (Figure 5a), and dFISH analysis (Figure 5d). The conclusion that A-P signals arise in non-cycling compartments (C106) is well-supported by the overlap analysis (Figure 5b). The negative result (C112) is important for ruling out a simple model of neck-restricted pluripotent stem cells.

results.result: Bulk-cell transplants from wild-type donors can rescue lethally irradiated tapeworms, and this rescue ability depends on cycling cells, as demonstrated by the failure of hydroxyurea-treated donor cells to rescue. This suggests tapeworm cycling cells contain bona fide stem cell activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114, C119-C120 are supported by cell transplantation experiments (Figure 6a-c) with appropriate controls (buffer injection, HU-treated donors). The rescue rate of 26% vs 1% for untreated vs HU-treated donors (C119) provides strong evidence for cycling cell requirement. However, the low rescue efficiency and technical challenges noted suggest the assay could be optimized.

results.result: Cells from both anterior (regeneration-competent) and posterior (regeneration-incompetent) regions can rescue lethally irradiated tapeworms. Posterior cycling cells can differentiate into multiple cell types including muscle/tegument and flame cells, showing hallmarks of stem cell activity despite being in non-regenerative tissue.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are supported by transplantation experiments (Figure 6b-c) and pulse-chase experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). The ability of posterior cells to rescue and differentiate into multiple lineages is critical evidence that stem cells are not restricted to the neck. The pulse-chase data showing differentiation into specific cell types strengthens the stem cell interpretation.

results.result: The regeneration competence of the neck is due to head-dependent extrinsic signals that create a permissive microenvironment for stem cell-driven regeneration, rather than intrinsic properties of neck-localized stem cells. The head and neck environment provide cues that regulate stem cell ability to regenerate proglottids, even though cycling cells are not anatomically confined.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C11, C125-C127 represent the main conclusion of the study, supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) neck is necessary and sufficient for regeneration (C6, C59), (2) head is required for persistent regeneration (C65), (3) cycling cells are distributed throughout the body (C76), (4) posterior cells can rescue when transplanted to the neck (C121-C122). This represents a well-supported model of extrinsic regulation of regeneration.

results.result: Transplanted cycling cells from donors can establish colonies, proliferate, and differentiate into terminally differentiated tissues at the animal edge in irradiated hosts, as shown by F-ara-EdU pulse-labeling experiments.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by pulse-labeling and transplantation experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1d). The detection of labeled cells in differentiated tissues provides direct evidence for stem cell engraftment and differentiation, though the low frequency of successful transplantations noted in the text suggests technical challenges.

results.result: Treatment with 50 mM hydroxyurea for 6 days resulted in 96±3% loss of cycling cells in H. diminuta.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is supported by quantitative data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1e-f) showing effective depletion of cycling cells by HU treatment. This provides a complementary method to irradiation for depleting cycling cells and validates the transplantation rescue assay.

results.result: Comparative analysis revealed that 38 verified tapeworm cycling-cell transcripts have conserved signatures with planarian neoblasts, with 22/28 putative planarian homologs showing enriched expression in neoblast-containing populations, despite >500 million years of evolutionary separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C140, C143-C147 are supported by dFISH validation of 38 transcripts and comparative analysis with published planarian datasets (Supplementary file 1c). The evolutionary conservation argument (C147) is well-supported by the data, though the analysis relies on sequence homology and expression pattern comparisons rather than functional conservation.

results.result: The cycling cell genes zmym3 and pogzl are neoblast cluster-defining genes in planarians, with the planarian homolog of pogzl (fir1) shown to be required for cell division and blastema formation after amputation, suggesting conserved functions in stem cell regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C153 are supported by comparative data (Supplementary file 1c) and citations to published planarian work (Han, 2018). The suggestion of conserved function (C151) is reasonable given the expression and functional data in planarians, though direct functional testing in tapeworms beyond the RNAi phenotypes would strengthen this claim.

results.result: This study demonstrated the first use of RNAi in H. diminuta, overcoming technical challenges that have limited adoption of RNAi in tapeworm biology despite previous demonstrations in other tapeworm species.
results.evaluation: Claims C158-C160 are supported by the successful RNAi experiments presented (Figure 4) with confirmed knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This represents a significant methodological advance for the field, enabling functional studies in H. diminuta.

results.result: A robust in vitro culture system was established for H. diminuta, modified from Schiller's method, allowing testing of regeneration from any amputated fragment for the first time.
results.evaluation: Claims C45 and C136 are supported by the successful culture and regeneration experiments throughout the study. The detailed methods section describes the culture conditions, and the results demonstrate that fragments can be maintained and regenerate in vitro for extended periods (up to 30 days). This methodological advance was essential for the study.

results.result: The authors propose models for how head-dependent signals may regulate regeneration: either by creating gradients that inhibit proglottidization in the neck, or by regulating a stem cell niche that maintains pluripotency. Alternative models consider whether the niche is head-dependent or independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C172 represent proposed models (Figure 6d-e) rather than tested hypotheses. While these models are consistent with the data presented, they are explicitly speculative and require future experimental validation. The models provide useful frameworks for future research but cannot be evaluated as supported or unsupported at this stage.

results.result: Tapeworms grow at rates rivaling the fastest-growing metazoan tissues, with H. diminuta producing up to 2200 proglottids, increasing in length by up to 3400 times and weight by up to 1.8 million times within the first 15 days of infection. This growth is fueled by adult somatic stem cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4, C21-C23 are supported by citation to Roberts, 1980 for the growth metrics and by the experimental data in this study demonstrating stem cell involvement in growth. The growth rates are extraordinary and well-documented in the literature, and this study provides molecular characterization of the stem cells driving this growth.

results.result: All amputated fragments (including body-only fragments) could grow in length and differentiate mature reproductive structures. Body-only fragments grew because existing proglottids increased in length as they matured, not through regeneration of new proglottids.
results.evaluation: Claims C49-C51 are supported by growth measurements (Figure 1d) and morphological analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a-b). This distinction between growth through proglottid maturation versus regeneration of new proglottids is important for understanding the regeneration-incompetent phenotype of body fragments.

results.result: Head regeneration was not observed in any case, and amputated heads alone could not regenerate either in vitro or in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C57 are supported by experimental observations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c) and citation to previous in vivo work (Read, 1967). This negative result is important for defining the limits of regenerative capacity in H. diminuta and contrasts with some planarian species that can regenerate heads.

results.result: The transcriptional heterogeneity detected in the H. diminuta cycling-cell compartment is reminiscent of observations in the regenerative planarian S. mediterranea, with conserved expression of transcripts in cycling-cell populations from these distantly related flatworms.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by the heterogeneity data from this study and comparative analysis with planarian datasets (Supplementary file 1c). The comparison is appropriate and strengthens the interpretation that tapeworm cycling cells include diverse stem and progenitor populations similar to planarians.
